ai.definition: Mind uploading is the hypothetical process of transferring a person’s consciousness from their biological brain into a digital format, such as a computer or other advanced computing system.
ai.howItWorks: The technique involves detailed mapping and simulation of the neural connections and patterns within an individual's brain. This could potentially be achieved through techniques like whole-brain emulation, where every neuron and its synaptic connections are replicated in a virtual environment.
ai.problemSolved: Preserving or transferring human consciousness to avoid death or for backup purposes, enabling digital afterlife experiences or long-term storage of minds.
ai.manufacturing: Current technology is not capable of achieving this. The necessary level of detail and accuracy required to map the brain's complex neural network does not exist yet.
ai.buildProcess: Requires advancements in neuroscience, computer science, and nanotechnology. It would involve creating a detailed model of the brain’s structure and function at the microscopic level, which is currently beyond our technological capabilities.
ai.costDrivers: High due to the complexity involved; requires significant investment in research, development, and potential ethical considerations around human subjects.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: Long-term future technology with current speculative status. Potential breakthroughs could make it more feasible in decades or centuries.
ai.regulation: No specific regulations exist for mind uploading as the technology does not yet exist at a viable level. Ethical and legal frameworks would need to be developed if and when the technology becomes possible.
ai.risks: Ethical, privacy, and safety concerns; potential loss of individual identity and consciousness; risks associated with data storage and security.
ai.profitability: Uncertain due to current speculative nature. If achieved, it could have significant implications for healthcare, digital preservation, and beyond, making it potentially highly profitable but also risky.
ai.futureDevelopment: Potential areas of development include advancements in neuroscience, artificial intelligence, nanotechnology, and data storage technologies that might enable more accurate brain mapping and simulation.

glossary.def: The process of replicating the structure and function of a human brain in a computer model.
A complex system of interconnected neurons that form the basis of brain functions, including memory and learning.
The detailed visualization and analysis of the structure and function of the brain using various imaging techniques.

subsystems.name: Brain preservation
subsystems.role: stabilise the brain's structure so it can be imaged without decay.

subsystems.name: Nanoscale imaging
subsystems.role: capture every neuron and synapse in three dimensions.

subsystems.name: Connectome reconstruction
subsystems.role: trace neural wiring from stacks of images.

subsystems.name: Functional state capture
subsystems.role: record synaptic strengths, receptor types and ongoing activity patterns.

subsystems.name: Computational simulation
subsystems.role: run a model of the reconstructed brain.

subsystems.name: Validation and interface
subsystems.role: test whether the simulation behaves like the person and give it senses or a body.

buildSteps.title: Preserve the brain
buildSteps.detail: After death, the brain is chemically fixed or vitrified to lock its structure in place before decay destroys it.

buildSteps.title: Slice and image
buildSteps.detail: The tissue is cut into thousands of nanometre-thin sections and imaged with electron microscopes to see every membrane and synapse.

buildSteps.title: Reconstruct the connectome
buildSteps.detail: Machine-learning algorithms trace each neuron and its connections from the images, with human proofreading to correct errors.

buildSteps.title: Capture functional properties
buildSteps.detail: Synaptic strengths, receptor types and neuromodulator levels must be measured or inferred; no current method can do this for a whole human brain.

buildSteps.title: Build a computational model
buildSteps.detail: The wiring diagram and functional data are converted into a simulation of neurons, synapses and their dynamics.

buildSteps.title: Run the simulation
buildSteps.detail: A supercomputer executes the model, requiring memory and processing far beyond today's largest machines to run in real time.

buildSteps.title: Validate and interact
buildSteps.detail: The simulated mind is tested for memory, personality and consciousness, and given sensors or a virtual body to interact with the world.

buildSteps.title: Transfer or store
buildSteps.detail: If successful, the mind could be copied, stored, or run in a different substrate — raising unresolved questions about identity.

prerequisites.why: complete wiring diagrams exist for a fruit fly and parts of mouse cortex, but not for a human brain.
current methods cannot measure the strength and type of every synapse in a human brain.
the largest supercomputers are approaching this scale, but simulating a human brain in real time is far beyond them.
there is no scientific consensus on what consciousness is or how to detect it in a simulation.
vitrification can preserve structure, but whether it retains functional information is unproven.

pathway.milestone: complete connectomes of small animals such as the fruit fly and parts of mouse cortex
pathway.unlocks: automated reconstruction methods and data-handling tools.

pathway.milestone: functional connectomics that links wiring to activity in mammals
simulation of a whole mouse brain
pathway.unlocks: proof that a detailed model can produce mind-like behaviour.
a substrate for uploading, if consciousness can be validated.
continuation of personal identity in a digital form — entirely unproven.
